sections.html:
Owensboro is the seat of Daviess County and Kentucky's fourth most populous city, along U.S. 60 and Interstate 165 roughly 107 miles southwest of Louisville. It counted 60,183 residents in 2020 and an estimated 60,892 on July 1, 2025, a rise of only 1.1 percent. The wider metro area, which also takes in Hancock and McLean counties, was estimated at 116,506.

The city sits in the crook of a bend in the Ohio River, 37 miles southeast of Evansville, Indiana. Workers spend a mean of 17.1 minutes getting to their jobs. Slow growth and a modest price level mean a house can sit if it is priced too high or needs work.

Median household income of $56,357 is a useful reference when deciding how far to price above the local median. At these values a repair bill can take a large share of a sale, which is part of why owners here sometimes prefer to sell as-is.

The median age was 38.1 in 2020, and 18.3 percent of residents were 65 or older. About 34.9 percent of households are one person, and 14.9 percent are one person aged 65 or older. A good share of sellers are older owners downsizing or heirs settling an estate. Of residents, 85.3 percent were in the same home a year before, and 29.0 percent of households had children under 18 at home.

The city has 26,918 housing units, 6.7 percent of them vacant in 2020. Owensboro's industrial past, from bourbon and tobacco to wagons, furniture and storage tanks, left a stock of older houses, and two distilleries, Glenmore and Green River, still operate.

Summers run hot and sticky and winters are moderately cold. Storms, tornadoes among them, can arrive in most months, and an F3 tornado cut through the city on December 9, 1952. Check the roof and gutters for storm damage before a house is shown.

The city enforces a Property Maintenance Code through Public Works. Ordinance 37-2019 amends the original 2011 ordinance and adopts provisions of the 2009 International Property Maintenance Code, and any violation counts as a nuisance. The code covers roughly 24,000 private parcels inside the city limits.

  • Code Enforcement Officers investigate, inspect and document conditions on a property.
  • A Notice of Violation comes first, with a citation after it.
  • Owners can appeal, and the city can abate a nuisance and enter property under the ordinance.

An empty or inherited house in poor shape should have its notices cleared before sale, or the buyer should be told what they cover. Cash buyers often take houses with deferred maintenance, since they plan the repairs themselves.

sections.h2: What a seller owes at the Daviess County Clerk
sections.html:
Daviess County Clerk staff record Owensboro deeds, and the seller settles Kentucky's transfer tax there under KRS 142.050: $0.50 on each $500 of value, with a partial unit counting in full.

A few transfers owe nothing, among them tax sales, partitions, divorce transfers between spouses, foreclosures and deeds in lieu. Call the clerk for the current recording fee, which can change, and ask the county PVA about your assessment and any exemption before you settle on a closing date.

sections.h2: Is a cash offer right for you?
sections.html:
Owensboro owners often hold older houses and face a small pool of showings, so a direct sale can save months. A cash buyer pays at closing and does not wait for a lender's appraisal, which helps when the roof, wiring or foundation needs work.

  • An estate where the owner has died or entered care and the family lives out of state.
  • A rental whose tenant left a damage list.
  • A property under a Property Maintenance notice the owner cannot afford to fix.
  • A move for work to Evansville, Louisville or elsewhere on a fixed date.

Request the offer in writing and ask who covers closing costs. Weigh the net against a listing after repairs, carrying costs and the transfer tax, and confirm any mortgage payoff with your lender.

Owensboro is a home rule city and has used a city manager form of government since 1954. Voters elect a mayor to a four-year term and four commissioners to two-year terms, and the commissioners hire a city manager who runs daily operations. Code, permit and utility questions go to city departments, not to the commission directly.

If you want to sell fast, collect what the buyer will want: the deed, any recorded liens, recent tax bills and notices from Code Enforcement. A clear file moves a sale to closing sooner whether the buyer pays cash or uses a lender.

When an owner has died or entered care, the family often lives elsewhere and wants a clean exit. Begin with the paperwork: the deed, recent tax bills, any recorded lien and every notice from Code Enforcement. Learn who is allowed to sign the deed, because the title search will ask. Then walk the property or send someone who can. Note storm damage, overgrown yard and anything that could draw a Notice of Violation.

If a notice is already open, read the fix or appeal deadline and decide whether to cure it or pass it to a buyer who plans repairs. Either way, tell the buyer what the notice covers. Ask the county PVA about the assessment and any exemption before you settle on a closing date, and call the clerk for the current recording fee.

1. Compare the offers by what you net, after payoff, transfer tax and repairs.
  2. Get the mortgage payoff from your lender in writing.
  3. Clear or disclose any Property Maintenance notice.
  4. Sign the contract and let the title search run.
  5. Sign the deed, pay the transfer tax at the clerk's counter and have the deed recorded.

A tenant-occupied house adds one more item: the lease and any damage list from a tenant who left. Hand both to the buyer, and keep a copy for yourself.

Once you have a contract, a title search checks the county records for liens, unpaid taxes and the mortgage. Each is paid from your proceeds, so get a payoff letter from the lender early. At the signing you sign the deed, pay the transfer tax at the clerk's office, and the clerk records the deed. A cash closing has no lender appraisal, so the date follows your schedule.

faqs.q: How big is the Owensboro metro area?
faqs.a: The city counted 60,183 people in 2020 and an estimated 60,892 on July 1, 2025. The metro area, including Hancock and McLean counties, was estimated at 116,506.

faqs.q: What tax applies when an Owensboro house sells?
faqs.a: Kentucky's transfer tax, paid by the seller at $0.50 per $500 of value, with the partial unit rounded up.

faqs.q: Who enforces upkeep standards in Owensboro?
faqs.a: Code Enforcement Officers under the city's Public Works department inspect, issue notices of violation and citations, and can abate nuisances.

faqs.q: Can an Owensboro house with a violation notice be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Read the notice, note the fix or appeal deadline and disclose it to the buyer. A cash buyer may take on the repair after closing.
The Daviess County Clerk, since the county records land for all its cities. Ask for the current recording fee before closing.
